name: Nora Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hughes and Son, a family garage on Mill Lane that's been there since the seventies. Mr Hughes took me on as an apprentice because he knew my dad from church, and I've stayed. I do servicing, exhausts, and I'm learning clutches, though I'm still slower than I'd like. I love the old customers who bring cakes at Christmas, and I hate the computer that plugs into the new cars, because it never says anything useful to me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Tom, who drives lorries for a builders' merchant, and we're getting married next summer at our church. We rent a small terrace and we're trying to save for the wedding, so there's under a month of money put by. My pay is low, but Mr Hughes is loyal, and there's not much else in town for a junior mechanic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, and that I never trusted all the fuss. Hard work and a good trade still count. I'd say that after church to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relieved, but it doesn't make the wedding cheaper. Mr Hughes is getting on, and his son works in an office in the city and doesn't want the garage. So I don't know how long Hughes and Son lasts, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep learning clutches from Mr Hughes. We'd keep the wedding small, maybe the church hall instead of the hotel. I'd keep away from the computer side as much as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a small worry about Mr Hughes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the garage when Mr Hughes stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. His son would probably sell the land. I've thought about asking if I could rent the workshop, but I'd never have the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the wedding. What gets cut if money's tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hotel, definitely, and the band. My aunties will do the wedding food. Church hall weddings are lovely anyway, my parents had one.

say: I never trusted **the fuss**, and hard work and a good trade still count.
I'd say that **after church** to anyone who asked.
think: I'm **relieved**, but it doesn't make the wedding cheaper.
Mr Hughes's son **doesn't want** the garage, so its future is uncertain.
do: Keep learning **clutches** from Mr Hughes and carry on as I am.
Hold the wedding in the **church hall** instead of the hotel.
Stay away from the **computer side** as much as possible.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a small worry about **Mr Hughes**.
S0.quote: My aunties will do the wedding food. Church hall weddings are lovely anyway, my parents had one.
fieldNote: Nora's job rests on **loyalty**: a family friend took her on through church.
Her real uncertainty is **succession**, since Mr Hughes's son won't take over.
She'd happily trim the **wedding** rather than take risks.

steps.text: Keep learning clutch work from Mr Hughes
Move the wedding reception from the hotel to the church hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the big companies chasing profit again, and ordinary people pay. Families and small firms like Hughes and Son get squeezed. I'd say that to anyone, I'm not shy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me. If the computer side does the quoting and the fault-finding, garages want people who can work the screen, and I'm hopeless at it. And Tom's firm already talks about software planning the lorry routes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hughes and Son and work harder on the spanner side, so I'm worth keeping for the hands-on jobs. I wouldn't do a computer course, I'd just get worse at it. Tom and I would push the wedding back a year so we have more saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into worried. Like a storm on the forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't do a computer course. What if Mr Hughes asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my boss Mr Hughes asked me to do a computer course, I'd do it for him, out of respect. He's done everything for me. My heart wouldn't be in it, though, and I wouldn't say no to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if things went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family first, and church. My dad's a carpenter and he'd always find me a few days' work. I'd rather that than any government scheme.

say: It's the **big companies** chasing profit, and ordinary people pay.
Families and **small firms** like Hughes and Son get squeezed.
think: Garages will want **screen skills**, and I'm hopeless at them.
Software already plans routes at **Tom's firm**, so his job feels shakier too.
do: Work harder on **spanner skills** to stay useful for hands-on jobs.
Avoid a **computer course** unless Mr Hughes asks.
**Push the wedding** back a year to save more.
feel: **Uneasy** turning into worried, like a storm on the forecast.
S1.quote: If my boss Mr Hughes asked me to do a computer course, I'd do it for him, out of respect. He's done everything for me.
fieldNote: Nora blames **big companies** and turns to family and church, not government.
She'd only retrain out of **loyalty** to her boss.
Both she and **Tom, a lorry driver**, face thinking-AI pressure here.

steps.text: Practise more hands-on repair work at Hughes and Son
Push the wedding back a year with Tom
Ask her dad for carpentry days if garage hours drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, and that people in charge let tech companies run wild. I'd say we need to look after our own, families and churches. I wouldn't post much online, but I'd say it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I think I'm in trouble. Quoting and diagnosis go to machines in 2028, so a garage needs fewer people. By 2031 a robot can do a clutch, and I'll be thirty-one with no other trade and a husband whose lorry drives itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Hughes and Son as long as Mr Hughes would have me. Tom and I would marry in the church hall, small, and not wait. I'd ask my dad to teach me carpentry on Saturdays, because fitting kitchens feels safer than cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be praying a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why marry sooner rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everything's going to change, I want to be married before it does. Family is the one thing a robot can't take. Waiting for money that might never come is daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said robots can do a clutch by 2031. Wouldn't they do kitchens too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably, you're right. Maybe a bit later, every house is different. I just don't know what else to do.

say: This is **wrong**, and people in charge let tech companies run wild.
We need to **look after our own**, families and churches.
think: Quoting and diagnosis go in **2028**, so the garage needs fewer people.
By **2031** robots do clutches, and Tom's lorry may drive itself.
do: Keep working at **Hughes and Son** while Mr Hughes will have me.
**Marry Tom** soon in a small church hall wedding.
Learn **carpentry** from my dad on Saturdays.
S2.quote: If everything's going to change, I want to be married before it does. Family is the one thing a robot can't take.
fieldNote: The fast timeline makes Nora **bring the wedding forward**, not delay it.
Her fallback, **carpentry** with her dad, admits its own weakness when challenged.
Both incomes face **automation**, and she has no clear plan.

steps.text: Keep working at Hughes and Son while there's work
Marry Tom soon in a small church hall wedding
Learn kitchen fitting from her dad on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've had a warning, so government should protect apprenticeships and family businesses, not just big tech. I'd say it at church and in the pub. I don't do politics online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years isn't long when you're as slow as me. Thinking AI by 2031, robots by 2034, I'd be thirty-four. And if Tom's job goes first, we'd be on one wage with a baby, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Hughes to teach me everything he knows in the next two years, the old cars especially, because collectors will want a person. We'd marry next summer as planned, small. I'd put whatever we can in savings and not take holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd keep my head up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said collectors would want a person. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A man with a 1970s sports car doesn't want a robot touching his car. He wants someone who knows the sound of it. That's the bit of the trade I'd want to be in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that enough work to live on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not, I don't know. There's a classic car club near us, maybe a dozen members. It would be thin.

say: Government should **protect apprenticeships** and family businesses, not big tech.
I'd say it at **church** and in the pub, not online.
think: Five years isn't long when you're **as slow** as me.
By **2034** I'd be thirty-four, maybe on one wage with a baby.
do: Ask Mr Hughes to teach me **old cars** over the next two years.
S3.quote: A man with a 1970s sports car doesn't want a robot touching his car. He wants someone who knows the sound of it.
fieldNote: Nora sees a niche in **classic cars**, then admits it may be too thin.
Her plans revolve around **family timing**: wedding, baby, one wage.
She stays alarmed because she judges herself **too slow** to retrain in time.

steps.text: Learn classic car repair from Mr Hughes over two years
Save all spare money and skip holidays
Hold a small wedding next summer as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do things properly: apprenticeships, families helping each other, not handouts. I'd say it to anyone. That's how my dad's generation got through things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a relief compared to the others. Robots in 2039, I'd be thirty-nine, and maybe I'd have kids at school by then. I still don't know what I'd do after, but there's time to find out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning from Mr Hughes and maybe, in a few years, ask to rent the workshop when he retires. Tom and I would marry next summer and start saving for a house. I'd learn the old cars and leave the screens to someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but a little worry stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Renting the workshop. Would you need a loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, which I hate. I'd rather my family pitched in, Tom's brother does books for small businesses. We'd see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd leave the screens to someone else. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a younger apprentice, if I had one. I'd take an apprentice on, the way my boss Mr Hughes took me. That's how a trade should pass on.

say: Ten years is time to do things **properly**: apprenticeships and families helping each other.
That's how **my dad's generation** got through hard times.
think: It's a **relief** compared to the faster pictures.
Robots in **2039** mean I might have kids at school by then.
do: Ask to **rent the workshop** when Mr Hughes retires in a few years.
Marry next summer and **save for a house**.
Learn **old cars** and leave the screens to an apprentice.
S4.quote: I'd take an apprentice on, the way my boss Mr Hughes took me. That's how a trade should pass on.
fieldNote: A decade lets Nora picture **running the workshop** herself.
She still dislikes **borrowing** and leans on family instead.
She'd hand the **screen work** to an apprentice, keeping her resistance.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hughes about renting the workshop when he retires
Save toward a house deposit with Tom

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Tom's lorry and my clutches both gone inside three years, and us just married. What would help is keeping apprenticeships going, with real people teaching real trades, and help for family businesses like Hughes and Son.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. It matters to me. Whatever happens with the robots, I've got a church full of people who'd turn up with a casserole.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens with the robots, I've got a church full of people who'd turn up with a casserole.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old** junior at Hughes and Son, a family garage where she apprenticed.
She is engaged to Tom, a **lorry driver**, and saving for a church wedding with under a month put by.
She avoids the **computer side** of repairs and never uses AI tools.
She leans on **family and church**, and blames big companies rather than ordinary people.
Her mood rises to **alarmed** with faster AGI, as both household incomes look exposed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with Tom's lorry job and her garage work gone in three years.
whatWouldHelp: Protected **apprenticeships** and support for **family businesses** like Hughes and Son.
